slides.title: Modeling language with computers
slides.content: Modeling language with computers • From a scientific point of view • computational linguistics • study of production, comprehension, and acquisition of linguistic phenomena from a computational perspective • From an engineering point of view • natural language processing • use computers to do useful things with language, e.g. question answering, sentiment analysis, machine translation 2/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Three paradigms
slides.content: Three paradigms • symbolic approach • knowledge-based approach to language modeling • handcrafted dictionaries and grammars • statistical approach • statistics and machine learning • large annotated corpora, handcrafted features • neural approach • neural networks • large (un)annotated corpora, no feature engineering 3/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: The role of linguistics
slides.content: The role of linguistics • How can linguistic phenomena be modeled computationally within the three aforementioned paradigms? • how to model words? • how to model sentences? • construction of meaning representation • How might linguistic theory be harnessed to improve natural language processing applications? 8/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Animal vs. human communication
slides.content: Animal vs. human communication • Features of human language • Interchangeability • Cultural transmission • Arbitrariness • Discreteness • Displacement • Productivity • Some are shared with animal communication systems, while others are (as far as we know) exclusively human 18/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Vervet monkey
slides.content: Vervet monkey • Uses arbitrary signs in order to signal predators • Not just utterances of stress or excitement • Signs have stable external reference and serve the purpose of communication • Three signs for different predators: • short, two syllable coughing sound • barking/peeping sound • continuous clicking, ‘chutter’ sound 19/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Vervet monkey
slides.content: Vervet monkey • Uses arbitrary signs in order to signal predators • Not just utterances of stress or excitement • Signs have stable external reference and serve the purpose of communication • Three signs for different predators: • short, two syllable coughing sound presence of an eagle →looking up and seeking shelter • barking/peeping sound presence of a leopard →escape in the trees • continuous clicking, ‘chutter’ sound presence of a snake →stand up and look down 19/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Human language: discreteness
slides.content: Human language: discreteness • Signs are composed of discrete, meaningless units, which can be combined in various ways to create new signs with different meanings stop [s·t·o·p] →spot tops opts • Animal communication systems mostly make use of signs that are indivisible units • This feature of human language is also called duality of patterning or double articulation 20/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Human language: displacement
slides.content: Human language: displacement • Humans can talk about things not present in space or time last night, a man on the moon, a unicorn, in September 2037, … • Animal communication systems are restricted to the present, the here and now 21/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Human language: productivity
slides.content: Human language: productivity • Humans can produce (and understand) an infinite amount of utterances apple, the apple, the green apple, the green apple that I ate last night, the green apple that I ate last night when I was… • in novel and creative ways e-mail, brexit, tiktokification, … • phonemes →morphemes →words →phrases → sentences • Animal communication: one utterance, one sign (vervet monkey) 22/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Compositionality
slides.content: Compositionality • Principle of compositionality (Frege): the meaning of an utterance is derived from the meaning of the signs and the way those signs are combined (1) Jim drives the car. (2) The car drives Jim. • Co-compositionality: the influence that signs exert on each other when they are combined (3) red rose (4) red wine (5) red hair 23/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: How to make sense of human speech?
slides.content: How to make sense of human speech? • Segmenting the utterance in terms of the basic units of sound and meaning • Recognizing how the basic units are composed into larger units (syntax) • Deriving the meanings of complex signs (compositional semantics) • Contextualizing the meanings so that full interpretations arise 24/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Linguistics
slides.content: Linguistics • Linguistics is the study of language • Linguistics is concerned with all aspects of how humans use language, and what they must know in order to do so • Linguistics asks different types of questions: • How are languages structured? • How are languages used? • How do languages change? 25/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: A brief history of linguistics
slides.content: A brief history of linguistics • India: description of Sanskrit (Panini) • Greece/Rome: description of ancient Greek (Latin) for rhetorical purposes • Middle ages: 7 arts – trivium (grammar, logic, and rhetorics) & quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and music) • Renaissance: attention for other languages than Greek and Latin; standardization of speech and writing 26/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Birth of linguistics as a science
slides.content: Birth of linguistics as a science • 1786: William Jones hints at common root of Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin, and other European languages • 19th century : historical and comparative linguistics (Brothers Grimm) Indo-European *ph2ter Sanskrit pitar Latin pater FR père SP padre IT padre West-Germanic DE Vater NL vader EN father 27/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: The Indo-European Language Family
slides.content: The Indo-European Language Family Proto-Indo-European Celtic Brythonic Welsh Gaelic Irish Gaelic Balto-Slavic Slavic Polish Russian Romance Latin French Italian Proto-Germanic East-Germanic Gothic West-Germanic Dutch English North-Germanic Danish Swedish 28/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: First half of the 20th century
slides.content: First half of the 20th century • Structuralism • Ferdinand de Saussure • signifiant vs. signifié, arbitrariness of the sign • the meaning of signs is determined by the other signs within the language structure • Descriptive linguistics • Edward Sapir, Benjamin Whorf, Leonard Bloomfield • study of native American languages, with emphasis on the differences • linguistic relativity: grammatical systems and language use affect perception 29/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Noam Chomsky
slides.content: Noam Chomsky • Generative grammar • Grammar as a system of rules that generates the grammatical sentences (and only those) for a given language • competence vs. performance • linguistic universals • need for formalization and full explicitness • Language acquisition device • discrepancy between • apparent complexity of natural languages • ease with which children acquire them • language is innate 30/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Relevance for our course
slides.content: Relevance for our course • Computational linguistics has been greatly influenced by Chomskyan formalization • More recently: implicit revisiting of earlier theories (structuralism) • What is it that makes language difficult for computers? • A complex phenomenon that involves the interaction of various types of knowledge and skills • Language understanding has to cope with an ubiquitous property of natural languages: ambiguity 31/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Levels of linguistic structure
slides.content: Levels of linguistic structure • phonology: sounds • morphology: structure of words • syntax: structure of sentences • semantics: the meaning of words, and how they combine to form larger meanings • pragmatics: the meaning of utterances within a discourse context 32/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Ambiguity: phonology
slides.content: Ambiguity: phonology • homophones : buy, by, bye • important for speech recognition 33/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Ambiguity: morphology
slides.content: Ambiguity: morphology • homonyms/homographs: • flies (noun) / flies (verb) • past (preposition) / past (noun) • like (preposition) / like (verb) • complicates syntactic analysis • complicates semantic analysis • when combined, the ambiguity becomes even more important • Time flies like an arrow. • Fruit flies like a banana. 34/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Ambiguity: syntax
slides.content: Ambiguity: syntax Structural ambiguity John hits the ball with a bat NP-SBJ DEP NP-OBJ PP DEP NP John hits the man with a hat NP-SBJ DEP NP-OBJ PP DEP NP 35/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Ambiguity: semantics
slides.content: Ambiguity: semantics • Leslie used a pen to write this letter. • We put he pigs in a pen. • The judge sent them to the pen for a decade. • They should pen that letter quickly. 36/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Ambiguity: pragmatics
slides.content: Ambiguity: pragmatics • Joe is the husband of Jill. His office is oval. • Joe called Jill . The first lady came in 5 minutes later . • The monkeys did not eat the bananas because they were not hungry. • The monkeys did not eat the bananas because they were not ripe. 37/48 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be
